title: The practices you keep
tomorrow: why do kids learn the end of the Qur'an first?

cards: The departures board flips from on time to delayed, then delayed again. Somebody groans. A toddler sleeps across three seats.

A man in a suit paces with his phone pressed to his ear. And in the corner by the window, a young woman lays her jacket on the carpet, checks a direction on her phone, and begins to pray. Nobody stops.
Nobody stares for long. A few minutes later she folds the jacket, sits back down and opens a granola bar. The flight is still late.
But something in her day just left exactly on time.

teach.b: Five practices have come up this whole hill with you. Prayer, salah, at its set times. Dhikr, remembering God with a word on the tongue.
Du'a, asking, in your own words. Fasting, the hunger that teaches. And giving, what leaves your hand for someone else.
None of them is big. That's the point.
The Qur'an puts prayer on a clock: "worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers." A clock doesn't care whether your flight left.
And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, asked which deeds God loves most, said the ones done constantly, even if they're small. Big gestures fade. Small ones, kept, become the shape of a life.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the Qur'an plans for the delayed traveler. When you go out into the land, it says, it's no sin to shorten the prayer.
Fasting has the same give: a traveler or someone sick can make up the days later. And the Prophet said the earth itself was made a place of prayer, so a jacket on an airport carpet will do.

teach.h: BUILT TO BEND, SO THEY HOLD.
teach.b: The practice bends so it can hold.
Dhikr fits in a line at the gate. Du'a needs no mat at all. Giving can be a seat offered to a tired parent.
The five don't wait for a perfect day. They're built for the airport, the dorm, the hospital hallway.

how: Muslims pray at set times through the day, wherever they are, often on a prayer mat or any clean cloth; travelers may shorten some prayers, and many keep dhikr, du'a, fasting and giving as small daily or weekly habits.

games.q: what does “the practices you keep” mean?
o: habits you'll start once life calms down
the small daily worship you keep for life
the rules you keep only in Ramadan

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.
p: no sin to shorten prayer on a journey

s: the Qur'an expects a traveler to pray exactly as at home
it says it's no sin to shorten the prayer when you go out into the land (4:101).
in a hadith, the deeds God loves most are the constant ones, even if small
Sahih al-Bukhari 6464: constant, even if little.
you need a proper prayer mat for the prayer to count
the Prophet said the earth was made a place of prayer; any clean place will do.

games.q: your cousin starts a job with long night shifts and says she'll get back to her practices 'when life calms down.' what fits today's idea?
o: wait for a calm season, then start again in a big way.
keep them small, and fit them into the shifts as they are.
drop the daily ones and keep one long session on her day off.
games.why: the hadith prizes the constant over the big, and the Qur'an bends prayer and fasting for travelers so they can be kept. small and steady holds.

practice: Picture the rest of today as a departures board, and give each of the five a slot: a prayer at its time if you pray, a line of remembrance while you wait for something, one honest ask, one craving you let pass, one small thing given.
Then find the one most likely to get delayed, and choose now where it goes instead.

wordCard.voice: The practices you keep: prayer, dhikr, du'a, fasting, giving. Small, set in the day, and made to travel.

orig.note: Arabic: the prayer, kept at its set times.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: the practices hold, even when the flight doesn't. Three of fifteen at the summit.
